title: Sets and unique items
summary: Keep only one copy of each item with a set. Count distinct card numbers, check membership, and learn why set order is not the main idea.
introduction: Suppose you collect cards numbered 4, 4, and 7. You own three cards but only two different numbers. A set helps a program remember which different items it has seen.
learningObjectives: Explain why duplicate items do not increase a set
Count unique items and check membership
Separate a set rule from the way it is stored

blocks.text: A **set** keeps at most one copy of each distinct item. **Distinct** means different. A **duplicate** is another copy of an item already present.
**Membership** asks whether an item is in the set. That answer matters more than an item's position. Do not depend on every language printing a set in the same order.

A set is a behavior, not one required storage plan. JavaScript Set, Python set, Java HashSet, and C# HashSet provide set operations. C++ std::set uses a tree. Our tiny C version checks an array by hand.

items: Add 4. Try to add 4 again; the set still has one item.
Add 7. The set now has two distinct items.
Print the size, 2. Check whether 7 is present and print 1 for yes.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

blocks.text: The two 4s count as one distinct value. The second line is a number so every language prints the same form: 1 means present and 0 means absent. No program depends on the order of set items.
Check the small and tricky cases
An empty set has size 0 and contains no item. Adding an existing number does not change its size. This lesson uses whole numbers so equality is easy to see.

The hand-made C membership check scans up to n stored items, so it is O(n). Tree-based C++ std::set lookups take O(log n), meaning the work grows slowly as the tree grows. Hash-based sets aim for O(1) average lookup, but collisions can make a lookup slower. The shared set rule does not promise one speed for all implementations.

items: Change the last input number from 7 to 4, but keep the membership question about 7.
The lines become 1 and 0. Only the distinct number 4 remains, and 7 is absent.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not use a set when you need to count every copy. A set of 4, 4, 7 cannot tell you that 4 appeared twice. Use a map of counts for that task.
